Transcript: During the Second World War, navy ships began using sonar to measure the depth of the sea, and the operators kept running into something strange. In deep water, far from any coast, an echo came back from a few hundred meters down, as if the ocean had suddenly turned shallow. People called it a false bottom, or a phantom bottom, and for a while nobody could say what it was.

Then someone noticed that the false bottom moved. A biologist, Martin Johnson, pointed out in the mid-1940s that the layer rose toward the surface around dusk and sank again around dawn. Rock doesn't do that. Animals do. We now know the layer is made of living things, small fish, shrimp-like krill, relatives of jellyfish, that spend the day down in the dark, where they're hard for predators to see, and come up at night to feed. It's thought to be one of the largest daily movements of animals anywhere on the planet.

So the mystery was solved. But here's the part that still causes trouble. Researchers wanted to use the same echoes to measure how much life is down there, and the echo turns out to be a poor scale. Sound bounces strongly off gas. Many small fish have a gas-filled swim bladder, and some of those jellyfish relatives carry a little gas float, and these can send back an echo far out of proportion to the animal's size. Meanwhile, fish whose bladders are filled with fat instead, or that have no bladder at all, may barely register.

That's one reason estimates of how much fish lives in this middle layer of the ocean have differed by as much as tenfold. The echo told us the layer was alive. It doesn't, on its own, tell us how much is there.

Transcript: Here's a classic demonstration from Jean Piaget. Take a baby of about nine or ten months. Hide a toy under cloth A, right in front of her, and she'll reach out and find it. Do that a few times. Then, while she watches, hide the toy under cloth B, a little to one side. Many babies reach back to A. They saw the toy go under B, and they still search where they found it before. It's called the A-not-B error.

Piaget's explanation was about knowledge. The infant, he argued, doesn't yet understand that an object goes on existing on its own, apart from her actions. For her, the toy is, in a sense, the thing you get by reaching to A.

The observation has held up remarkably well. Labs all over the world reproduce it. What has held up less well is the explanation. The psychologist Adele Diamond noticed that some infants look at B, where the toy actually is, while their hand goes to A. Their eyes seem to know something their reach doesn't. She argued the difficulty is in holding back a well-practiced action, a skill tied to the front of the brain, which matures slowly.

Then Linda Smith, Esther Thelen, and their colleagues pushed further. They reported that the error can appear even with no toy at all, when infants simply reach for a lid that was waved in front of them. And small changes to the body could make it much weaker, for instance, standing the baby up for the B trials instead of keeping her seated.

If the error depends on posture, it's hard to treat it as purely a gap in what the baby believes about objects. So Piaget gave us a lasting fact and, quite possibly, the wrong reason for it. Much of the error seems to live in the reaching itself.

Transcript: Ask which building was the first skyscraper and you'll usually hear one answer: the Home Insurance Building in Chicago, finished in 1885 and designed by William Le Baron Jenney. It was about ten stories tall, which doesn't sound like much today, and it was torn down in 1931. Its claim rests on its frame. Instead of thick masonry walls holding everything up, much of the weight was carried by a skeleton of iron and, in the upper floors, steel.

Why does a frame matter so much? Because a masonry wall has to get thicker at the bottom the taller the building gets. Chicago's Monadnock Building, finished a few years later with load-bearing brick walls, has walls nearly two meters thick at street level. Go much higher that way and the ground floor is mostly wall. A frame removes that limit.

Now, the case for "first" is weaker than the plaque suggests. Iron frames inside buildings weren't new; English textile mills had used iron columns and beams decades earlier. Tall office buildings weren't new either; New York had office buildings with elevators in the 1870s. And historians who've looked closely point out that parts of the Home Insurance Building's outer walls were still heavy masonry, helping to carry the load. It was a hybrid.

So was it the first skyscraper? That depends entirely on what you decide the word means. If it means height, other buildings came first. If it means a frame doing all of the work, it may not qualify at all. What you can say is that it combined several existing ideas at a moment when Chicago, rebuilding after its great fire and short of space downtown, was ready to push them.

That's often how firsts in architecture work. The title goes to the building standing where the pieces happen to come together.

It was about ten stories tall, which doesn't sound like much today, and it was torn down in 1931. Its claim rests on its frame. Instead of thick masonry walls holding everything up, much of the weight was carried by a skeleton of iron and, in the upper floors, steel.

Why does a frame matter so much? Because a masonry wall has to get thicker at the bottom the taller the building gets. Chicago's Monadnock Building, finished a few years later with load-bearing brick walls, has walls nearly two meters thick at street level. Go much higher that way and the ground floor is mostly wall. A frame removes that limit.

Now, the case for "first" is weaker than the plaque suggests. Iron frames inside buildings weren't new; English textile mills had used iron columns and beams decades earlier. Tall office buildings weren't new either; New York had office buildings with elevators in the 1870s. And historians who've looked closely point out that parts of the Home Insurance Building's outer walls were still heavy masonry, helping to carry the load. It was a hybrid.

So was it the first skyscraper? That depends entirely on what you decide the word means. If it means height, other buildings came first. If it means a frame doing all of the work, it may not qualify at all. What you can say is that it combined several existing ideas at a moment when Chicago, rebuilding after its great fire and short of space downtown, was ready to push them.

That's often how firsts in architecture work. The title goes to the building standing where the pieces happen to come together.

Transcript: You've probably heard this one: in old European churches, the window panes are thicker at the bottom than at the top, because glass is really a very slow liquid, and over the centuries it has sagged. It's a great story. Let's take it apart, and then put one piece of it back.

First, the panes themselves. Before the nineteenth century, a lot of window glass was made by blowing a bubble, opening it up, and spinning it into a flat disc. That disc was never even; it was thicker in some places than in others. When glaziers cut panes from it, the panes were often uneven, and many put the heavy edge at the bottom, which makes sense for stability. But not all of them did. Old panes have been found with the thick edge at the top or off to one side, and sagging can't explain that.

Second, the rates. Scientists have estimated how fast ordinary window glass would flow at room temperature, and the answer is so slow that visible sagging would take far longer than the age of the universe. And there's a simpler check: Roman glass vessels, far older than any cathedral window, haven't slumped, and old telescope lenses still hold their precise shape.

So glass does not flow in any way that matters. But here's the piece I want to put back. The story wasn't pulled from nowhere. In a crystal, like quartz, the atoms sit in a regular repeating pattern. In glass, they don't; the arrangement is disordered, frozen in place as the melt cooled, rather like a snapshot of a liquid. That's why glass is called an amorphous solid, and it's why the liquid talk caught on.

The mistake was sliding from arranged like a liquid to behaves like a liquid. Structure and flow are separate questions.

Transcript: Brown-headed cowbirds never build a nest. A female lays her eggs in the nests of other species, and the hosts raise the cowbird chick, often at the cost of some of their own young. The obvious question is why so many hosts put up with it. Some species do throw foreign eggs out. Many don't.

One proposal, from the biologist Amotz Zahavi in 1979, sounded almost like a joke. He suggested that parasites might punish hosts that reject their eggs, by coming back and wrecking the nest. Accept the egg, and you raise a stranger but keep some of your own chicks. Reject it, and you might lose everything. It came to be called the mafia hypothesis. Plenty of people thought it asked too much of a bird: remembering which nests it had laid in and checking on them later.

Then, in 2007, Jeffrey Hoover and Scott Robinson tested it with prothonotary warblers in Illinois, which nest in boxes. From some nests they removed the cowbird eggs, so those hosts looked like rejecters. Those nests were destroyed far more often than nests where the cowbird egg was left alone. And when cowbirds were kept from getting back into the boxes, the difference went away. That points to cowbirds, not some other predator. A similar pattern had been reported earlier for a cuckoo and the magpies it uses in Spain.

So the skeptics were wrong about what a bird can manage. But notice how far the result reaches. It shows retaliation in one host, in one region, and that the threat there is real. It doesn't show that fear of punishment is why hosts accept eggs in general. Many accepters may simply fail to recognize the foreign egg, or find rejecting it too costly. For those species, the mafia story may have nothing to say.

Transcript: The letters on your keyboard come in a strange order: Q, W, E, R, T, Y across the top left. The arrangement goes back to typewriters of the 1870s associated with Christopher Latham Sholes, and the usual story is that it was meant to keep common letter pairs apart so the metal arms inside wouldn't jam.

In 1985 the economic historian Paul David made this layout famous in his field. His argument went roughly like this. In the 1930s August Dvorak patented a layout that put the most common letters on the middle row, and studies reported that typists trained on it were much faster. Yet nobody switched. Why? Because by then millions of typists had learned QWERTY, and employers bought machines to match the typists available. Each choice made sense by itself, and together they kept everyone on the worse design. Economists call this path dependence, or lock-in.

Then two economists, Stan Liebowitz and Stephen Margolis, went back to the evidence. They argued that the most cited study favoring Dvorak had been run under Dvorak's own influence, and that a later government study, in the 1950s, found that retraining typists on Dvorak gave no clear advantage over simply giving them more practice on QWERTY.

Notice what their critique does and doesn't show. It doesn't show that lock-in never happens; switching costs are real, and David was right that they can hold a standard in place. What it shows is that QWERTY, the textbook example, may not be a case of being stuck with something worse. The claim that our keyboards are inferior was never properly established.

That's a useful warning. A famous illustration can go on being repeated for decades after the evidence under it has worn thin.

Because by then millions of typists had learned QWERTY, and employers bought machines to match the typists available. Each choice made sense by itself, and together they kept everyone on the worse design. Economists call this path dependence, or lock-in.

Transcript: In June 1991, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines produced one of the largest eruptions of the twentieth century. It had been quiet for roughly five hundred years. And yet the death toll was far lower than it could have been, because scientists saw it coming. Teams from the Philippine volcano institute and the U.S. Geological Survey set up seismometers, measured the gas coming out of the vents, and watched the earthquakes grow more frequent and shallower. They raised the alert level step by step, and tens of thousands of people, including the staff of a large American air base nearby, were moved out before the climax. Estimates vary, but that warning probably saved thousands of lives.

So it's tempting to conclude that eruption forecasting is a solved problem. Watch the signals, and you'll know. But here's the other side. In 1982, after swarms of earthquakes and some uplift of the ground at Long Valley, a large volcanic area in eastern California, the Geological Survey issued a formal hazard notice. Nothing erupted. The nearby resort town of Mammoth Lakes saw its tourism drop, local people were furious, and some of the scientists became the target of real anger. Decades later, Long Valley still hasn't erupted.

Now, I don't think the lesson is that the Long Valley notice was a mistake. The signals there were genuine. The magma moved. It just stopped. And that's the hard part. Volcanoes show unrest far more often than they erupt, and our instruments are much better at telling us that magma is on the move than at telling us whether it'll reach the surface.

Pinatubo worked partly because, by the final days, the signs were escalating fast and all pointing the same way. In the early stages of unrest, which is exactly when people want answers, forecasters are mostly working with probabilities.

Transcript: You've probably heard that Eskimo languages have dozens, maybe hundreds, of words for snow. It's one of the most repeated facts about language, usually offered as proof that the words you have shape what you notice. Let's look at where it came from.

The anthropologist Franz Boas, writing in 1911, mentioned in passing that one of these languages had four separate roots for snow: snow on the ground, falling snow, drifting snow, and a snowdrift. His point was actually a modest one, that languages divide up the world differently. Later writers repeated the example, and the number grew. Dozens, and in some newspaper pieces, hundreds. In the 1980s, the anthropologist Laura Martin traced this chain of retellings, and the linguist Geoffrey Pullum later spread her findings in a well-known essay that called the whole thing a hoax. Nobody, it turned out, had gone back and counted.

So, case closed? Not quite. Some later fieldwork, especially on sea ice, has recorded fairly large sets of terms in certain Inuit and Yupik dialects. People who hunt and travel on ice really do need to talk about its kinds precisely. So the flat claim you sometimes hear from debunkers, that these languages have no more snow vocabulary than English, may go too far as well.

But here's the part I find most interesting. These languages build words by attaching many pieces to a root. One long word can express what English says in a whole sentence, something like "snow that is falling softly right now." So how many words for snow are there? Practically unlimited, because speakers can keep building new ones. Which means the count can't be compared with English in the first place. The retellings were wrong, yes. But the deeper problem was that the question itself was badly posed.

Transcript: The interval we call the tritone spans three whole steps, say from F up to B. Play those two notes together and you get a tense, restless sound that seems to want to go somewhere. And you may have heard that in the Middle Ages the Church banned it, calling it the devil in music, diabolus in musica.

It's a great story. As far as historians can tell, there's no evidence for it. No church decree forbidding the tritone has ever been found. And that Latin nickname doesn't seem to show up in writing until centuries later, around the early seventeen hundreds.

What is true is that medieval theorists told composers to avoid it, in melodies and between voices sounding together. But their reasons were technical. Singers then learned music through a system of overlapping six-note patterns, and the F and the B belonged to patterns that didn't fit together, so the leap between them was awkward to sing and awkward to think about. Theorists described it as mi against fa, which were the names those two notes had in the system. It was a matter of grammar, not of sin.

And here's the irony. A few centuries later, the very instability that made the tritone something to avoid became its most useful property. In the harmony of Bach's era and after, the dominant seventh chord, the chord that pulls you back home at the end of a phrase, has a tritone right inside it. The two notes resolve, moving by step to a stable interval, and that motion is a big part of what makes an ending feel like an ending.

So the tritone didn't go from forbidden to accepted because composers stopped fearing the devil. It always had to be handled with care. What changed was the musical system around it, which turned a problem into a tool.

Transcript: In the winter of 1944 to 1945, the German occupation cut off food supplies to the western Netherlands. Official rations in some cities fell well below a thousand calories a day, and thousands of people died. Then, in May 1945, the country was liberated and food came back quickly. Grim as it was, this created something unusual for researchers: a famine with a sharp beginning and a sharp end, in a population with very good birth records.

Decades later, researchers followed up people who had been in the womb during the famine. Some groups, depending on when in pregnancy the famine hit, showed higher rates of obesity and heart disease later in life. And in 2008, a study found that people exposed early in pregnancy carried different chemical tags, called methylation, on a gene involved in growth, about sixty years afterward. These tags don't change the DNA sequence. They affect how strongly genes are switched on or off.

That's a real finding, and it's where things get exciting, and sometimes overexcited. You'll read that the famine left its mark on the grandchildren, that hunger is passed down through generations like an inheritance. A few studies have reported effects in the next generation, though the results are mixed.

Here's the catch that's easy to miss. When a pregnant woman goes hungry, three generations are exposed at once: the woman, her fetus, and, if the fetus is a girl, the egg cells already forming inside it. A girl's eggs begin developing before she's born. So an effect in a grandchild doesn't have to be inherited at all. It could be a direct effect of the famine on cells that were already present during it.

To show true inheritance, you'd need effects in a generation that never met the famine in any form, the great-grandchildren. For humans, that evidence just isn't there yet.

Transcript: When the Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990, its first images were a disappointment. Stars that should have been sharp points came out surrounded by a fuzzy halo. The cause turned out to be the main mirror. It had been ground to the wrong shape. Near its edge it was too flat by about two micrometers, a tiny fraction of the width of a human hair. But in an instrument that demanding, that was enough to blur everything.

Now, here's the strange part. The mirror was one of the most precisely polished ever made. Its surface was smooth and consistent. It was just the wrong shape. Precise, and wrong.

How did that happen? The polishing was guided by a testing device, a kind of reference instrument that measured the mirror's curve while it was being ground. One lens in that device had been set out of position by a little over a millimeter. So the mirror was polished, very carefully, to match a faulty standard. And here's the painful bit. Simpler, cruder tests during manufacturing did show a problem. The investigation afterward found that those results were set aside, because the main device was considered far more reliable.

There's a happy ending, more or less. Because the error was so consistent, it could be measured exactly, and an error known exactly can be cancelled. In 1993, astronauts installed corrective optics, small mirrors shaped to offset the flaw, in effect giving the telescope glasses. Later cameras were built with the correction designed in.

The lesson people usually draw from this is that you should always check your work. I'd put it more narrowly. The work was checked. The trouble was that every disagreement got settled in favor of the one instrument everyone trusted most.

Transcript: In late August 1854, cholera broke out in Soho, in central London, and within about ten days, hundreds of people living near Broad Street were dead. The physician John Snow mapped the deaths and found them clustered around one public water pump. He persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump's handle, and, so the story goes, the outbreak stopped. It's often told as the founding moment of epidemiology.

Here's the problem with that story. By the time the handle came off, on September eighth, the number of new cases was already falling. Snow himself said so. Many residents had fled, and the outbreak may well have been burning out on its own. So if you ask whether removing the handle ended the epidemic, a skeptic would say the evidence is thin, and the skeptic would have a point.

But the handle was never Snow's strongest evidence. That came from what he called a grand experiment. In south London, two water companies served the same streets, sometimes houses right next door to each other. One drew its water from the Thames downstream of the city's sewage. The other had moved its intake upriver, to cleaner water. The households were alike in almost every way except their water. Snow went door to door finding out which company supplied each house, and the death rate among customers of the downstream company turned out to be many times higher.
